citeAs: Lu, Pan, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, and Jianfeng Gao (2024). MathVista: Evaluating Mathematical Reasoning of Foundation Models in Visual Contexts. ICLR 2024.
creator: Pan Lu, Hritik Bansal, Tony Xia, Jiacheng Liu, Chunyuan Li, Hannaneh Hajishirzi, Hao Cheng, Kai-Wei Chang, Michel Galley, Jianfeng Gao
description: MathVista is a benchmark for evaluating mathematical reasoning in visual contexts. It consolidates 28 existing multimodal datasets and 3 newly created datasets into 6,141 examples spanning diverse tasks, visual contexts, and mathematical reasoning types.
name: MathVista
publisher: UCLA, University of Washington, Microsoft Research
rai:annotatorDemographics: Graduate students in STEM fields annotated the new datasets. Human performance annotators on Amazon Mechanical Turk were required to have a high school diploma or higher, a satisfactory annotation history, and to pass qualification examples.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: For the 736 newly collected questions, independent annotation by three reviewers achieved a 99.2% inter-annotation consistency rate, with only 6 disagreements resolved by team discussion. For labeling whether examples involved mathematical reasoning, the paper reports a Fleiss Kappa of 0.775 among three annotators. For mathematical reasoning labels, 94.1% of examples from automatic and human annotations had the exact same set of reasoning types, and 98.79% of individual labels were identical.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: For filtered VQA examples, three expert annotators manually labeled whether examples involved mathematical reasoning, with majority voting used for finalization. For the three new datasets, all questions were manually annotated by graduate students in STEM fields and then refined through a two-step review process in which each dataset was independently annotated by three reviewers and disagreements were resolved by discussion among the entire review team. Metadata such as question type, answer type, language, source, category, task, grade level, and visual context was obtained from source dataset details, and mathematical reasoning labels were automatically assigned then checked by expert annotators on a 1,000-example sample.
rai:dataBiases: The paper notes possible gaps in representation of certain types of mathematical problems and visuals. It also notes that source annotations come from heterogeneous original providers and lack a unified format and structure, and that only 85.6% of examples have annotations.
rai:dataCollection: The benchmark was compiled by collecting 9 existing multimodal MathQA datasets, reviewing more than 70 VQA datasets and selecting 19 public datasets with math-related instances, and creating 3 new datasets: IQTest, FunctionQA, and PaperQA. For VQA sources, heuristic rules first selected likely math-related examples, then expert annotators manually labeled whether they involved mathematical reasoning; source datasets were limited to up to 400 examples for balance.
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper notes that only 85.6% of examples have annotations because annotations were sourced from original data providers, and that answer labels for the test subset will not be publicly released to prevent data contamination.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: The raw/source data consists of examples drawn from 31 source datasets, including existing multimodal MathQA and VQA datasets, plus newly sourced puzzle test figures from online learning platforms, functional plots, and academic paper figures including tables, figures, and charts from online education resources and papers on Huggingface.
rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Web Scraping
rai:dataLimitations: The authors note limitations in dataset coverage, including possible gaps in certain types of mathematical problems and visuals, labor-intensive collection that may limit scalability and generalizability, heterogeneity and lack of unified format in sourced annotations, and potential data noise. They also note that only 85.6% of examples have annotations.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The compiled benchmark balances source representation by limiting each source dataset to up to 400 examples. For release, the dataset was split into testmini and test using a two-stage random sampling strategy: first sampling up to 4 questions per source dataset, then sampling remaining questions according to each source's overall proportion in the full set.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For general VQA datasets, heuristic rules automatically selected examples likely to involve mathematical reasoning by choosing examples with numeric answers or quantity words in the question. False positives were then removed through manual expert labeling. Each source dataset was capped at up to 400 examples to balance representation, and the benchmark was split into testmini and test by random sampling designed to preserve source-dataset distribution. The authors also conducted several quality checks to address unidentified errors.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is positioned as supporting the development of general-purpose AI agents capable of tackling mathematically intensive and visually rich real-world tasks, including educational disciplines, statistical analysis, theorem proving, and scientific discovery.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended as a benchmark for evaluating and developing AI systems, especially large language and multimodal models, for mathematical reasoning in visual contexts. It is meant to facilitate model development, systematic evaluation, and future research on general-purpose AI assistants for visually rich and mathematically intensive tasks.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Heuristic rules were used to automatically select likely math-related examples from VQA datasets, based on numeric answers and quantity words. Automatic annotation was also used for coarse mathematical reasoning labels, which was later verified by expert annotators on a sample.
